title: Doing tasks in order
objectives: Order tasks with dependencies by topological sort.
Detect a cycle when no valid order exists

screens.title: A nightly pipeline
screens.prose: Each arrow means the first task must finish before the second starts. A backtest needs signals and risk limits; both need returns.
screens.question: Put the tasks in an order that respects every arrow.

hints.text: Which tasks have no arrow coming in? They can go first.
returns waits for both prices and calendar.
prices and calendar first, either way round. Then returns, then signals and risk, then backtest, then report.

feedback.correct: Every arrow points forward in your order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each task must come after every task with an arrow into it.

byKey.returns: returns needs both prices and calendar first.
byKey.backtest: backtest needs signals and risk, so both come before it.
byKey.report: report is last: it needs the backtest.

explain.text: Four orders work: prices and calendar either way round, and signals and risk either way round. An order in which every arrow points forward is a **topological order**. A graph of arrows with no loop is a **DAG**, a directed acyclic graph.

screens.title: Arrows in
screens.prose: For each task, count the arrows that point into it: how many tasks it waits for.
screens.question: Fill in each task's count.

hints.text: Count only arrowheads touching the task.
returns has two arrows in, from prices and calendar.
prices 0, calendar 0, returns 2, signals 1, risk 1, backtest 2, report 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count arrowheads, not lines leaving the task.

byKey.r2c1: returns has arrows in from prices and calendar: 2.
byKey.r5c1: backtest waits for signals and risk: 2.
byKey.r0c1: prices has an arrow out, but none in.

explain.text: This count is the **in-degree** from lesson 1. A task with in-degree 0 is free to start now. Finishing a task lowers the in-degree of every task it points to.

screens.title: Who is free now
screens.prose: prices, calendar and returns have run. Their arrows are gone, so the counts they fed have dropped.
screens.question: Tap every task that can start now.

hints.text: Which remaining tasks have no arrow coming in?
signals and risk waited only for returns.
signals and risk now have in-degree 0. backtest still waits for both of them.

feedback.correct: signals and risk are both free, in either order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the tasks with no arrow left pointing in.

byKey.backtest: backtest still has two arrows in, from signals and risk.

explain.text: That is **Kahn's algorithm**: keep the tasks with in-degree 0 in a queue, take one, and remove its arrows. Any task whose count hits 0 joins the queue. Repeat until the queue is empty.

screens.title: Kahn's algorithm in code
screens.prose: `adj` maps every task to the tasks that need it. When several are free, take the alphabetically smallest, so each graph has one answer: a `heapq` does this. If tasks are left over, there is a cycle.

state.caption: Expected: calendar, prices, returns, risk, signals, backtest, report

screens.question: Write `topo_sort(adj)`: one valid order, ties to the smallest name, or `None` if there is a cycle.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, including a graph with no edges, a two-task cycle, a self-loop and an empty graph. Every task is a key; ties go to the smallest name; return `None` on a cycle.

hints.text: Count in-degrees first. Then repeat: pop the smallest free task, record it, lower its successors' counts.
calendar beats prices: both are free and c comes before p.
`ready = [u for u in adj if indeg[u] == 0]`, `heapify` it; `heappop`, append, decrement each `v` in `adj[u]`, push it at 0. Return `None` if `len(order) < len(adj)`.

feedback.correct: In-degrees, a heap of free tasks, and a length check for cycles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 wants the smallest free name each time. A plain queue keeps arrival order, so risk lands after signals; use `heapq`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is a two-task cycle. Nothing is ever free, so the order is empty: return `None`, not `[]`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is the empty graph: no tasks, so the order is `[]`.

explain.text: Each task is pushed and popped once, and each arrow lowers one count once. That is $O(V + E)$, or $O(V \log V + E)$ with the heap. A task on a cycle never reaches in-degree 0, so it is never emitted.

screens.title: Starting in the wrong place
screens.question: Which task does `order` start with?

options.why: You expected it to start from a task with nothing to wait for. The loop starts from the first name alphabetically, whatever its in-degree.
prices is a fine first task, but the loop never checks in-degrees: it starts with the smallest name.
report is reached from backtest, so it comes second.

hints.text: What is the first name in `sorted(adj)`?
b comes before c and p.
`sorted(adj)` starts with backtest, so `visit("backtest")` runs first and records it before signals or risk exist.

feedback.correct: It runs the backtest before any of its inputs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where the outer loop starts.

byKey.calendar: You assumed the loop starts with a free task. It starts with the smallest name, backtest, which has in-degree 2.
byKey.prices: You assumed the loop checks what is free. It never looks at in-degrees.

explain.text: The full result is backtest, report, calendar, returns, risk, signals, prices: backtest runs first, before its inputs. Recording on arrival is pre-order, which only follows arrows forward from wherever it starts. Either start from in-degree 0 (Kahn), or use post-order, next.

canvas.caption: backtest emitted before signals and risk

screens.title: Post-order, reversed
screens.prose: Move `order.append(u)` below the loop, so each task is recorded when its call **finishes**. The outer loop is unchanged.
screens.question: Put the tasks in the order they are appended.

hints.text: The first call is `visit("backtest")`. What must finish before it does?
report has no arrows out, so its call finishes first.
report, backtest. Then calendar's call runs returns, risk and signals: risk, signals, returns, calendar. prices is last.

feedback.correct: Every task is appended after all the tasks that need it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A call finishes only after every call it starts.

byKey.backtest: backtest's call starts report's first, so report is appended before backtest.
byKey.risk: From returns the calls go to risk, then signals, in sorted order.
byKey.prices: prices is tried last by the outer loop: its only arrow leads to returns, already done.

explain.text: In post-order each task comes after everything that depends on it. Reversed, every task comes before its dependents: prices, calendar, returns, signals, risk, backtest, report. That is a valid order, from any starting point.

canvas.caption: Reversed post-order: a valid run order

screens.title: A loop in the pipeline
screens.prose: Someone adds an arrow from backtest to risk: risk now needs backtest results, while backtest still needs risk.
screens.question: How many tasks does Kahn's algorithm emit before it stalls?

hints.text: Run the counts forward. Which tasks ever reach in-degree 0?
risk and backtest each wait on the other.
calendar, prices, returns and signals are emitted. risk keeps one arrow in, from backtest, and backtest keeps one from risk.

feedback.correct: Four of seven: the cycle and report never start.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Emit tasks only when their count reaches 0.

byKey.all: A task on a cycle never reaches in-degree 0, so not all 7 can be emitted.
byKey.none: The cycle blocks only part of the graph. calendar and prices still start at 0.
byKey.five: risk still has an arrow in from backtest, so it is never free.

explain.text: Kahn's algorithm stops with 4 of 7 emitted. Fewer than $V$ emitted means a cycle: here risk and backtest, with report stuck behind them. That length check is how `topo_sort` returns `None`.

screens.title: Ordering by dependencies
screens.prose:
```python
indeg = in-degree of every node
ready = nodes with in-degree 0
while ready:
    take u from ready, append it to order
    for each v after u:
        indeg[v] -= 1; if 0, add v to ready
cycle if len(order) < V
```
This is $O(V + E)$. Reversed DFS post-order gives an order too, at the same cost.
screens.question: Kahn's algorithm emits 9 of a graph's 12 nodes and `ready` is empty. What do you conclude?

options.text: The other 3 nodes lie on a cycle or wait on one, so no valid order exists

options.why: A node with no edges has in-degree 0, so it is emitted at the start.

options.text: A second pass will emit them
options.why: Their counts can only fall when a prerequisite is emitted, and none of theirs can be.

feedback.correct: Leftover nodes always mean a cycle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask why a node's in-degree never reached 0.

explain.text: Every leftover node still has an arrow in from another leftover node. Following those arrows backwards must eventually repeat a node, which is a cycle.

screens.title: The overnight risk run
screens.prose: A risk system lists each job with the jobs it needs first. Raw inputs such as `positions` are never listed as jobs themselves. The scheduler needs one run order.

state.caption: The overnight VaR run: arrows point from a job to what needs it

screens.question: Write `run_order(deps)`: every job and raw input in a valid order, ties to the smallest name, or `None` on a cycle.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. `deps` maps each job to the jobs it needs first; a job named only as a prerequisite is a raw input and must appear too. Ties go to the smallest name; return `None` on a cycle.

hints.text: Turn each `job: [prerequisites]` into arrows from each prerequisite to the job.
market_data and positions appear only as prerequisites, yet they belong in the order.
Collect every name into `jobs`. Build `after[p].append(job)` and `indeg[job] += 1`, then run Kahn's algorithm with a heap.

feedback.correct: Reverse the arrows, include the raw inputs, then Kahn's algorithm.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 needs the raw inputs market_data and positions in the order. Add every prerequisite as a node.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is a cycle of two jobs: return `None`.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 is one job with no prerequisites: `["report"]`.

explain.text: The order is market_data, positions, scenarios, pnl_vectors, var_report, limits_check. The input listed prerequisites, so the arrows run the other way from `adj`. Forgetting raw inputs leaves them out and breaks the length check.

ideas: A topological order puts every task after all its prerequisites. It exists only when the graph has no cycle, and often there are several.
Kahn's algorithm keeps the tasks with in-degree 0, emits one, and lowers its successors' counts. Fewer than $V$ emitted means a cycle.
Reversed DFS post-order is also a valid order. Pre-order is not: it can emit a task before its inputs.

formula.name: Topological sort
formula.note: Each task emitted once; each arrow lowers one count once.

summary.trap: Starting from a task that still has arrows in, or emitting on arrival, runs a task before its prerequisites.

quiz.prose: Four tasks with no arrows between them at all.
quiz.question: How many valid orders are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no arrows, nothing constrains the order.

byKey.one: With no arrows nothing forces one order. Every arrangement is valid.
byKey.four: That counts the tasks. The orders are the arrangements of 4 tasks: $4!$.

explain.text: No arrow means no constraint, so every arrangement is valid: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$. Kahn's algorithm with name ties returns just one of them.

quiz.prose: Arrows: a → b, a → c, c → b.
quiz.question: Which order is valid?

options.why: b needs c first: the arrow c → b.
c needs a first: the arrow a → c.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every arrow against your order.

explain.text: a has in-degree 0, so it goes first. Then c is free, and b needs both a and c. The only valid order is a, c, b.

quiz.prose: The DFS method for ordering tasks reverses the post-order.
quiz.question: Why reverse it?

options.text: Post-order lists every task after the tasks that depend on it, so reversing puts prerequisites first
It is already valid; reversing just breaks ties
options.why: Post-order put report before backtest, which report needs. It must be reversed.
Reversed post-order is not pre-order: pre-order emitted backtest before its inputs.

feedback.correct: A call finishes only after everything it leads to.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which tasks finish before a given task's call does.

explain.text: A task's call finishes after the calls of every task it points to. So in post-order dependents come first, and the reverse puts each task before its dependents.

quiz.question: What is the in-degree of q?

feedback.correct: p, r and s point into q.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count only arrows ending at q.

byKey.all: You counted every arrow touching q. (q, t) leaves q, so it is not counted.
byKey.out: That is q's out-degree, the arrow to t.

explain.text: Three arrows end at q: from p, r and s. So q waits for three tasks.
